To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a model for lung incidence based on smoking history and the underlying age distribution explains a significant portion of the observed trends, and that the effect of smoking on lung cancer risk is multiplicative.

(1) a sizeable proportion of the period and the cohort effects in the lung cancer incidence data can be explained by a simple smoking model; (2) a multiplicative effect is a better model for the period and the birth cohort effects than a model that considers smoking history as a non-multiplicative effect; and (3) the model is sensitive to the assumptions made about the relationship between smoking and lung cancer.
the model for the effect on smoking on lung cancer in Connecticut is a mixture of the multiplicative and non-multiplicative models.
